24   decided to adopt the name). CCA claims that BBK and CCA are not competitors because 
25   CCA’s  products  contain  cannabis,  while  none  of  BBK’s  products  do,  and  that  its 
26   merchandise is merely incidental to CCA’s brand. (Doc. 485 at 15.) Undisputed facts show, 
27   however, that CCA knew of the RAW brand and that the Raw Garden products are 
28   complementary to BBK’s RAW brand. John De Friel, CCA’s chief executive officer, knew 
1   of BBK’s RAW branded rolling papers since 2005 (Doc. 496-14 at 4), and in 2014, CCA 
2   and others posted images of RAW rolling papers on social media in conjunction with Raw 
3   Garden cannabis (Docs. 496-15, 496-16). CCA also reached out to BBK in 2017 about the 
4   possibility of the RAW branded cones being printed with “Raw Garden.” (Doc. 485-20 at 
5   20-24.) Furthermore, CCA even notes in its papers that the Court previously found that 
6   some  of  BBK’s  products  use  the  RAW  mark  on  of  its  “federally-illegal  drug

8        On balance, the Court finds the undisputed material facts show that the E-System 
9   factors weight in favor of BBK and show that the delay was reasonable. As such, laches 
10   does not bar BBK’s trademark claims.                                 
11        Therefore, with respect to the laches defense, the Court grants BBK’s motion 
12   (Doc. 478 at 7-18) and denies CCA’s motion (Doc. 485 at 11-17).      
13             2.   Statute of Limitations                                
14        BBK  and  CCA  both  move  for  summary  judgment  on  whether  the  statute  of 
15   limitations ran on BBK’s Arizona common law infringement and unfair competition 
16   claims. (Doc. 478 at 19-20; Doc. 485 at 17.)                         
17        Both claims are subject to a three-year statute of limitations. See Ranch Realty, Inc. 
18   v. DC Ranch Realty, LLC, 614 F. Supp. 2d 983, 989-90 (D. Ariz. 2007). Yet, under the 
19   doctrine of continuing tort, “a tort claim based on a series of related wrongful acts is 
20   considered continuous, and accrual begins at the termination of the wrongdoing, rather than 
21   at the beginning.” Crus v. City of Tucson, 243 Ariz. 69, 74 (App. 2017). 
22        Here, the fact that BBK did not file the claims until September 18, 2019, outside the 
23   three-year statute of limitations, does not preclude BBK’s state-law claims in their entirety. 
24   See 4 McCarthy on Trademarks and Unfair Competition § 31:33 (4th ed.) (“Usually, 
25   infringement is a continuing wrong, and the statute of limitations is no bar except as to 
26   damages beyond the statutory period.”). Rather, the claims are limited to the three-years 
27   preceding the filing of the lawsuit. See, e.g., Novell, Inc. v. Unicom Sales, Inc., No. C-03-
28   2785 MMC, 2004 WL 1839117, at *4 (N.D. Cal. Aug. 17, 2004).          
1        Therefore, with respect to statute of limitations, the Court grants BBK’s motion 
2   (Doc. 478 at 19-20) and denies CCA’s motion (Doc. 485 at 17) as a matter of law. BBK’s 
3   Arizona  common  law  infringement  and  unfair  competition  claims  are  limited  to  the 
4   three-year time period before September 18, 2019.                    
5        B.   CCA’s Other Defenses                                       
6        BBK moves for summary judgment on CCA’s remaining affirmative defenses 
7   (1) acquiescence, (2) waiver, (3) estoppel, (4) unclean hands, and (5) other defenses. 
8             1.   Acquiescence                                          
9        “Acquiescence, as a defense to trademark infringement, requires that (1) the senior 
10   user actively represented that it would not assert a right or a claim, (2) the delay between 
11   the active representation and assertion of the right or claim was not excusable, and (3) the 
12   delay caused the defendant undue prejudice.” PetConnect Rescue, Inc. v. Salinas, 656 F. 
13   Supp.  3d  1131,  1180  (S.D.  Cal.  2023)  (emphasis  added).  Acquiescence  requires  an 
14   affirmative word or deed conveying consent to use the trademark. Seller Agency Council, 
15   Inc. v. Kennedy Ctr. for Real Est. Educ., Inc., 621 F.3d 981, 988-89 (9th Cir. 2010). 
16        For similar reasons that the laches defense fails, the Court finds CCA’s acquiescence 
17   defense must also fail. As discussed, no evidence suggests that BBK actively represented 
18   it would not assert its right in the RAW mark. In fact, BBK contested CCA’s use of Raw 
19   Garden with the USPTO in 2017. Also, as discussed, the Court found the three-month delay 
20   in filing the lawsuit reasonable.                                    
21        The Court therefore grants BBK’s motion (Doc. 478 at 18) with respect to the 
22   acquiescence defense.                                                
23             2.   Waiver                                                
24        “A waiver is an intentional relinquishment or abandonment of a known right or 
25   privilege.” United States v. Amwest Sur. Ins. Co., 54 F.3d 601, 602 (9th Cir. 1995) (citation 
26   omitted). The “waiver must be manifested in an unequivocal manner.” Monster Energy Co. 
27   v. BeastUp LLC, 395 F. Supp. 3d 1334, 1367 (E.D. Cal. 2019). “An implied waiver of 
28   rights  will  be found where there is ‘clear, decisive and unequivocal’ conduct which 
1   indicates a purpose to waive the legal rights involved.” Amwest Sur. Ins. Co., 54 F.3d at 
2   602-03.                                                              
3        CCA presents evidence that BBK representatives (1) learned of the Raw Garden at 
4   the 2016 Chalice Cup festival and discussed potential collaboration because each had the 
5   word “Raw” in their name and exchanged merchandise and business cards (Doc. 485-14 at 
6   18-20) and (2) made social media posts “shout[ing] out to @raw_garden” (Doc. 486-7). 
7   CCA also contacted BBK for pricing of the RAW rolling papers because “we had had a 
8   positive interaction with one of their reps at [the] Chalice [Cup] the year before.” (Doc. 
9   485-20 at 7.)                                                        
10        BBK argues that there is no evidence in the record of a  “clear, decisive and

24   October 10, 2016, and has used them for its Raw Garden business since. (Doc. 485-11 at 
25   5-17.) The rawgarden.farm website is used to provide information about CCA’s farming 
26   and cannabis products, and the rawgarden.co website is used to sell merchandise. (Doc.

2        Cybersquatting occurs when “a person other than the trademark holder registers the 
3   domain name of a well[-]known trademark and then attempts to profit from this by either 
4   ransoming the domain name back to the trademark holder or by using the domain name to 
5   divert business from the trademark holder to the domain name holder.” Bosley Med. Inst., 
6   Inc.  v.  Kremer,  403  F.3d  672,  680  (9th  Cir.  2005).  The  primary  elements  of  a 
7   cybersquatting claim under the Anti-Cybersquatting Consumer Protection Act (“ACPA”) 
8   are: “(1) the defendant registered, trafficked in, or used a domain name; (2) the domain 
9   name is identical or confusingly similar to a protected mark owned by the plaintiff; and (3) 
10   the defendant acted with bad faith intent to profit from that mark.” Rearden LLC v. Rearden 
11   Com., Inc., 683 F.3d 1190, 1219 (9th Cir. 2012) (internal quotations omitted).

13   whether bad faith exists.” Lahoti v. VeriCheck, Inc., 586 F.3d 1190, 1202 (9th Cir. 2009).

24             disparage the mark, by creating a likelihood of confusion as to

25

26             domain name to the mark owner or any third party for financial

27             domain name in the bona fide offering of any goods or services,

28             conduct;

21   at 20-22.) CCA argues that as a matter of law that BBK’s profit disgorgement theory should 
22   be rejected because CCA’s purported profits are derived from the sale of federally illegal 
23   cannabis products, which violates the Controlled Substances Act (“CSA”), 21 U.S.C. 
24   §§ 801, et seq. (Id. at 21.)                                         
25        The CSA makes it unlawful for any person “to manufacture, distribute, or dispense” 
26   a controlled substance. 21 U.S.C. § 841(a). It designates cannabinoids as a Schedule I 
27   controlled substance. Id. § 812. Courts have found against awarding damages from profits 
28   earned on business that process and sell cannabis. See, e.g., J. Lilly, LLC v. Clearspan 
1   Fabric Structures Int’l, Inc., No. 3:18-cv-01104-HZ, 2020 WL 1855190, at *12 (D. Or. 
2   Apr. 13, 2020) (refusing to award lost profits to a plaintiff who alleged that defendant’s 
3   conduct caused plaintiff to lose profits on its own illegal cultivation and sale of marijuana). 
4   Courts acknowledge, however, that “[t]he mere fact of marijuana’s involvement does not 
5   by itself automatically preclude [the party] from seeking redress. As the [c]ourt recognized 
6   in  the  prior  ruling, case  law suggests  no  such hard-and-fast  rule.”  Sensoria,  LLC  v. 
7   Kaweske, 548 F. Supp. 3d 1011, 1026-28 (D. Colo. 2021) (dismissing claims based on 
8   theft, fraud, negligent misrepresentation, breach of fiduciary duty, civil conspiracy, unjust 
9   enrichment, and securities claims reasoning the court could not “vindicate equity in or 
10   award profits from a business that grows, processes, and sells marijuana”). 
11        CCA concedes that no court has addressed this issue specifically in the context of 
12   trademark infringement. (Doc. 485 at 21.) In one unpublished case, a district court found 
13   that an award of profit disgorgement would “run afoul of federal law.” Wildflower Brands 
14   Inc. v. Camacho, No. 2:22-CV-09044-MCS-PLA, 2023 WL 3150091, at *2 (C.D. Cal. 
15   Mar. 20, 2023). Yet, Wildflower Brands can be distinguished because it was a breach of 
16   contract dispute between two cannabis companies. See id. at *1. In fact, most cases cited 
17   by CCA are distinguishable, because both parties were engaged in the federally illegal 
18   cannabis industry. See, e.g., Sensoria, 548 F. Supp. 3d at 1026-28; J. Lilly, 2020 WL 
19   1855190, at *12. Here, however, only CCA operates in this space.     
20        BBK alleges that CCA violated its lawful trademark rights with its legal products. 
21   In the cases cited by CCA, the courts decline to award damages when doing so would 
22   benefit the party violating CSA federal law. If the jury finds CCA infringed on BBK’s 
23   trademark, BBK may seek profit disgorgement—allowing CCA to be immune from a 
24   damages claim would incentivize, not discourage, the violation of federal criminal law. 
25        The Court therefore denies CCA’s motion (Doc. 485 at 20-22) as to BBK’s claim 
26   for profit disgorgement.

11   Steinway & Sons Inc., 497 F. Supp. 3d 479, 515 (D. Ariz. 2020) (quoting Dawson v. 
12   Withycombe, 216 Ariz. 84, 111 (Ct. App. 2007)); see also Dawson, 216 Ariz. at 112 (“[A]n 
13   evil hand guided by an evil mind which either consciously sought to damage the victim or 
14   acting intentionally, knowing that its conduct was likely to cause unjustified, significant 
15   damage  to  the  victim motives  so  improper, or  conduct  so  oppressive,  outrageous or 
16   intolerable that such an evil mind may be inferred.”) (cleaned up).

18   rolling papers since 2005. (Doc. 496-14 at 4.) And, in 2014, CCA posted images of RAW

27   at 12-13).)

19   doctrine of continuing tort, “a tort claim based on a series of related wrongful acts is

21   at the beginning.” Crus v. City of Tucson,
243 Ariz. 69
, 74 (App. 2017).

25   infringement is a continuing wrong, and the statute of limitations is no bar except as to

27   preceding the filing of the lawsuit. See, e.g., Novell, Inc. v. Unicom Sales, Inc., No. C-03-
28   2785 MMC,
2004 WL 1839117
, at *4 (N.D. Cal. Aug. 17, 2004).

9        “Acquiescence, as a defense to trademark infringement, requires that (1) the senior 
10   user actively represented that it would not assert a right or a claim, (2) the delay between 
11   the active representation and assertion of the right or claim was not excusable, and (3) the 
12   delay caused the defendant undue prejudice.” PetConnect Rescue, Inc. v. Salinas,
656 F. 13

14   affirmative word or deed conveying consent to use the trademark. Seller Agency Council, 
15   Inc. v. Kennedy Ctr. for Real Est. Educ., Inc.,
621 F.3d 981, 988-89
 (9th Cir. 2010). 
16        For similar reasons that the laches defense fails, the Court finds CCA’s acquiescence 
17   defense must also fail. As discussed, no evidence suggests that BBK actively represented 
18   it would not assert its right in the RAW mark. In fact, BBK contested CCA’s use of Raw 
19   Garden with the USPTO in 2017. Also, as discussed, the Court found the three-month delay 
20   in filing the lawsuit reasonable.                                    
21        The Court therefore grants BBK’s motion (Doc. 478 at 18) with respect to the 
22   acquiescence defense.                                                
23             2.   Waiver                                                
24        “A waiver is an intentional relinquishment or abandonment of a known right or 
25   privilege.” United States v. Amwest Sur. Ins. Co.,
54 F.3d 601, 602
 (9th Cir. 1995) (citation 
26   omitted). The “waiver must be manifested in an unequivocal manner.” Monster Energy Co. 
27   v. BeastUp LLC,
395 F. Supp. 3d 1334
, 1367 (E.D. Cal. 2019). “An implied waiver of 
28   rights  will  be found where there is ‘clear, decisive and unequivocal’ conduct which 
1   indicates a purpose to waive the legal rights involved.” Amwest Sur. Ins. Co.,
54 F.3d at 2
   602-03.                                                              
3        CCA presents evidence that BBK representatives (1) learned of the Raw Garden at 
4   the 2016 Chalice Cup festival and discussed potential collaboration because each had the 
5   word “Raw” in their name and exchanged merchandise and business cards (Doc. 485-14 at 
6   18-20) and (2) made social media posts “shout[ing] out to @raw_garden” (Doc. 486-7). 
7   CCA also contacted BBK for pricing of the RAW rolling papers because “we had had a 
8   positive interaction with one of their reps at [the] Chalice [Cup] the year before.” (Doc. 
9   485-20 at 7.)

11   unequivocal” manifestation of its intent to relinquish any of its trademark rights. (Doc. 478 
12   at 19.)

14   a material disputed fact that BBK expressed “clear, decisive and unequivocal conduct” to 
15   relinquish or abandon its trademark rights. Nothing about BBK’s behavior is decisive or

18   impacting BBK’s legal rights. To the contrary, as discussed, BBK opposed CCA’s 2017 
19   application to the USPTO—showing BBK’s intent to defend its trademark rights. See, e.g., 
20   Monster Energy Co., 395 F. Supp. 3d at 1367 (finding the defendant provided no evidence

26        “Unlike waiver, estoppel focuses not on a party’s intent, but rather on the effects of 
27   his conduct on another. Estoppel arises only when a party’s conduct misleads another to

546 F. Supp. 2d 1029
, 
2   1075 (D.  Or.  2008).  CCA  must  prove:  (1)  BBK  knew  CCA  was  selling  potentially

7   if BBK is allowed to proceed with its claim. See
id.

23        CCA  registered  the  “rawgarden.farm”  and  “rawgarden.co”  domain  names  on 
24   October 10, 2016, and has used them for its Raw Garden business since. (Doc. 485-11 at 
25   5-17.) The rawgarden.farm website is used to provide information about CCA’s farming

28   with the California Secretary of State to use the Raw Garden mark, and in the application, 
1   CCA indicated that it had been using the mark since 2016. (Doc. 485-26; Doc. 485-27.) 
2        Cybersquatting occurs when “a person other than the trademark holder registers the 
3   domain name of a well[-]known trademark and then attempts to profit from this by either 
4   ransoming the domain name back to the trademark holder or by using the domain name to 
5   divert business from the trademark holder to the domain name holder.” Bosley Med. Inst., 
6   Inc.  v.  Kremer,
403 F.3d 672, 680
  (9th  Cir.  2005).  The  primary  elements  of  a 
7   cybersquatting claim under the Anti-Cybersquatting Consumer Protection Act (“ACPA”) 
8   are: “(1) the defendant registered, trafficked in, or used a domain name; (2) the domain 
9   name is identical or confusingly similar to a protected mark owned by the plaintiff; and (3) 
10   the defendant acted with bad faith intent to profit from that mark.” Rearden LLC v. Rearden 
11   Com., Inc.,
683 F.3d 1190, 1219
 (9th Cir. 2012) (internal quotations omitted). 
12        The ACPA lists “nine nonexclusive factors for courts to consider in determining 
13   whether bad faith exists.” Lahoti v. VeriCheck, Inc.,
586 F.3d 1190, 1202
 (9th Cir. 2009). 
14   These factors are:                                                   
15             (I) the trademark or other intellectual property rights of the 
              person, if any, in the domain name;                        
16                                                                        
              (II) the extent to which the domain name consists of the legal 
17             name of the person or a name that is otherwise commonly used 
              to identify that person;                                   
18                                                                        
              (III) the person’s prior use, if any, of the domain name in 
19             connection  with  the  bona  fide  offering  of  any  goods  or 
              services;                                                  
20                                                                        
              (IV) the person’s bona fide noncommercial or fair use of the 
21             mark in a site accessible under the domain name;           
22             (V) the person’s intent to divert consumers from the mark  
              owner’s online location to a site accessible under the domain 
23             name that could harm the goodwill represented by the mark, 
              either for commercial gain or with the intent to tarnish or 
24             disparage the mark, by creating a likelihood of confusion as to 
              the source, sponsorship, affiliation, or endorsement of the site; 
25                                                                        
              (VI) the person’s offer to transfer, sell, or otherwise assign the 
26             domain name to the mark owner or any third party for financial 
              gain  without  having  used,  or  having  an  intent  to  use,  the 
27             domain name in the bona fide offering of any goods or services, 
              or  the  person’s  prior  conduct  indicating  a  pattern  of  such 
28             conduct;                                                   
1             (VII) the person’s provision of material and misleading false 
              contact information when applying for the registration of the
